title: Mysticorum Expositiones Sacramentorum Seu Quaestiones In Vetus Testamentum
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1409.tmp1409.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: 12. Cum vero albam, illos haereticos qui se mundos appellant, sive reliquos, qui de falso merito gloriantur, sicut Pelagius et Novatus. Cum autem macram vel lividam lepram commemorat, invidiae et livuris notas exsecratur. Cum vero nigram insinuat, sacrificiorum fumo et busto idololatriae denigratam conscientiam detestatur.
passages.english: 12. But when [it mentions] white [leprosy], [it means] those heretics who call themselves the pure, or the others who boast of false merit, such as Pelagius and Novatus. And when it mentions thin or livid leprosy, it curses the marks of envy and spite. But when it suggests black [leprosy], it denounces a conscience blackened by the smoke of sacrifices and the pyre of idolatry.
passages.notes: The first sentence is elliptical, with the verb implied from the preceding section, which is not given. "Livuris" is presumably for "livoris" (of spite). "Novatus" may refer to Novatian, founder of the Novatianist schism; the two were often confused.

passages.original: 2. De qua quaestione beatæ memoriæ Augustinus episcopus Simpliciano Mediolanensi episcopo ita scripsit : lnquiria, inquam, utrum potuerit malignus spiritus excitare animam justi, et tanquam de abditis mortuorum repagulis, vel receptaculis evocare, et ut videre- tur, et loqueretur cum Saul.
passages.english: 2. On this question Augustine, the bishop of blessed memory, wrote thus to Simplician, bishop of Milan: "You ask," I say, "whether an evil spirit could have roused the soul of a just man, and called it forth as if from the hidden bars or receptacles of the dead, so that it was seen and spoke with Saul."
passages.notes: 'lnquiria' is read as 'Inquiris' (you ask), a scanning error. 'videre- tur' is read as 'videretur'. The punctuation of 'Inquiris, inquam' is awkward. The 'I say' may belong to Augustine's own phrasing as quoted.

passages.original: 6. Unde et cherubim, cum sint cœlestes virtutes, fictæ tamen 528 ex metallo, quod imperavit Deus super arcam Testamenti magnæ rei significandæ gratia, non aliud quam cherubim illa quoque figmenta vocabantur. Item dum quisque videt somnium, non dicit: Vidi imaginem Augustini, sed ; Vidi Augustinum, cum eo tempore quo aliquod tale aliquis vidit ignoraret hoc Augustinus.
passages.english: 6. Hence also the cherubim: although they are heavenly powers, yet those figures made of metal, which God commanded [to be placed] over the ark of the Covenant for the sake of signifying a great matter, were also called nothing other than cherubim. Likewise, when anyone sees a dream, he does not say, "I saw an image of Augustine," but, "I saw Augustine," although at the time when someone saw some such thing, Augustine was unaware of it.
passages.notes: '528' is a page number of the printed edition and is omitted. 'quod imperavit' (singular) refers loosely to the plural figures.

passages.original: Sed, quoniam sive illud fieri possit, sive non possit, tamen fallacia Satanæ atque imaginum simulandarum callida operatio decipiendis sensibus humanis multiformis invigilat, pedetentim quidem, ne inquisitionibus diligentioribus præscribamus, sed tamen potius existimemus, tale aliquid factum maligno spiritu pythonissæ illius ministerio, quandiu nobis aliquid amplius excogitare atque explicare non datur. Haec sunt quæ tunc de pythonissa et Samuele scripsit beatissimus Augustinus.
passages.english: But whether that can happen or cannot, the deceit of Satan and the cunning, many-formed work of feigning images is ever watchful to deceive the human senses. So, step by step indeed, so as not to prejudge more careful inquiries, let us nevertheless rather suppose that something of this kind was done by an evil spirit through the agency of that pythoness, for as long as it is not given to us to think out and explain anything further. These are the things that the most blessed Augustine wrote at that time about the pythoness and Samuel.
passages.notes: 'Pythoness' renders 'pythonissa', the medium of Endor. The sentence 'Sed... invigilat' is grammatically loose and has been split in translation.
